Phones Belong Out of the Driver's Hands

Most people now carry a cell phone everywhere they go, and the car is no exception. The phone gives directions, plays music, and keeps us in touch with family and work. Because it is so useful, many drivers treat it as part of the dashboard. Even so, drivers should not hold or handle a phone at all while the vehicle is moving. The only use that makes sense is hands-free and set up before the trip starts, such as a navigation route that speaks out loud.

The main reason is attention. Driving looks routine, but it asks a lot of the brain. A driver has to watch the road ahead, check mirrors, judge the speed of other cars, and react to things nobody expects, like a child chasing a ball into the street. Reading a text takes about five seconds. At fifty-five miles per hour, a car covers roughly the length of a football field in that time. For those seconds the driver is basically blind. No message is important enough to justify that.

Some people argue that talking on the phone is no worse than talking to a passenger. Research does not back this up. A passenger can see the road too. When traffic gets tricky, a passenger usually stops talking or even warns the driver. The person on the other end of a call has no idea what is happening, so the conversation keeps pulling at the driver's attention right when it is needed most. Studies have found that even hands-free calls slow reaction times, because the problem is in the mind, not only in the hands.

Others point out that phones have become essential tools, especially for navigation. That is true, and it is the reason for the one exception. A driver can enter an address before leaving the driveway and let the phone give spoken directions from a mount. What should not happen is typing, scrolling, or picking up the device while the car is in gear. If the route needs changing, the driver can pull over. Taking thirty seconds in a parking lot costs almost nothing.

There is also a question of fairness to everyone else on the road. A driver who chooses to text is not only taking a risk with his or her own life. Pedestrians, cyclists, and other drivers never agreed to that risk. Laws already forbid drunk driving because impaired drivers endanger others, and distracted driving creates a similar danger. Clear rules against handheld phone use, backed by real penalties, send the message that the road is shared space.

Cell phones are not going away, and they do make daily life easier. Behind the wheel, though, the driver's job is to drive. Setting the phone down, or putting it in a do-not-disturb mode until the trip is over, is a small sacrifice. Compared with the lives it can protect, it is hardly a sacrifice at all.
